newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ First's Peters defends power stations sale.
newsitem.headline: NZ First's Peters defends power stations sale.

text.p: New Zealand First leader Winston Peters on Tuesday defended the coalition government's decision to sell off eight small power stations, saying compromises had to be made.

Peters was responding to Labour leader Helen Clark who said NZ First had betrayed its voters by allowing the sale to go ahead. NZ First campaigned in the October 1996 election on a strong platform of opposing state asset sales.
"We're in a new age now of MMP where we can't win every fight that we're involved in," Peters told National Radio.
It was understood the stations would pass to New Zealanders or local supply authorities or Maori.
"NZ First policy was no sale at all on anything of that sort but you can't win every fight. We had to compromise in the interests of forming a government," Peters said.
He said the sale had to meet the foreign investment rules set out in the coalition agreement.
"We would be looking at each sale by sale. Our foreign ownership policy is pretty stringent when it comes to important resources such as power."
Local authorities or power companies which had foreign ownership such as TransAlta would have to meet the law.
Peters said there was no intention to sell spur lines, which branch off the main grid and feed a small number of power stations.
Peters and State Owned Enterprises Minister Jenny Shipley on Monday confirmed the sale of the stations would go ahead, as decided by the last government.

The stations to be sold are: Matahina near Whakatane; Kaitawa, Tuai and Piripaua stations near Lake Waikaremoana (to be sold as one group); Mangahao near Levin; the Cobb station in Golden Bay; and the Coleridge and Highbank stations near Christchurch.
If any were not sold to either energy company or Maori interests after a defined period -- understood to be 18 months -- ownership would transfer to Contact Energy.
NZ First and the conservative National Party formed a coalition after October's general election.
The former National government first announced its intention to sell the eight stations, which together make up nearly four percent of New Zealand's generation capacity, in mid-1995.
